newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU/Britain row on BA alliance unearths legal mire.
newsitem.headline: EU/Britain row on BA alliance unearths legal mire.

text.p: Britain's latest row with the European Commission, over British Airways's planned deal with American Airlines, has prompted another visit to an already well-thumbed EU treaty and its less-than-clear diktats.

Behind recent days' bad-tempered exchanges between Britain's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and the European Commission lies a disagreement about who has the power to rule on the competition effects of the planned deal.
The definitive answer lies at the end of a drawn-out legal battle in the European Court of Justice. But that may not happen.
"This is new legal territory. In the end it would be up to the European Court to decide," one legal expert told Reuters.
Far more likely is that the current row about legal powers will be part of a noisy compromise allowing both parties to cry victory and the alliance to go ahead, albeit with some changes.

The wrangle has simmered since last July, when the Commission announced inquiries into six planned and existing transatlantic alliances after getting news of BA's draft deal with AMR Corp's American Airlines.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said the deal would dwarf all previous alliances, such as the one between Germany's Lufthansa and United Airlines, which the Commission had chosen to ignore precisely because of the legal uncertainties.

Van Miert acknowledged in July that because the alliances involved services spanning the 15-country bloc's external borders, a 1987 EU regulation 3975/87 applying EU competition laws to the air transport sector would not be enough to bring the bloc's competition powers into play.
These powers, defined in EU Treaty articles 85 and 86, cannot generally be used without implementing law and rules of procedure for the Commission.

"To investigate such cases, the Commission consequently has to use Article 89 of the Treaty," the EU executive said in a briefing note issued at the time. Article 89 includes a requirement that the Commission "ensure application of the principles laid down in Articles 85 and 86".

Britain contests the Commission's use of Article 89, arguing that any inquiry is for British authorities using powers set out in Article 88, which provides for national authorities to rule on the admissibility of potentially anti-competitive agreements or abuses of dominant positions.

A Brussels-based aviation expert told Reuters that Article 89 did provide the Commission with powers to invesitgate possible breaches of Articles 85 and 86 and cited the Commission's use of just such powers in 1986. The Commission used the article then to force 10 European Community carriers, including British Airways, to end practices it alleged to be restrictive.

Van Miert urged in his letter to Britain's DTI last Friday that London delay any approval of the BA/American deal or risk creating "a conflict with any decision of the Commission to prohibit the alliance".
His remarks related to a draft decision by Britain's Office of Fair Trading to clear the alliance if the carriers gave up 168 weekly take-off and landing slots at Heathrow.

The Commission has used identical legal arguments for its inquiries into the alliances involving Lufthansa and SAS with United and Delta Air Line's four-way tie up, without the corresponding slanging match breaking out.
A spokeswoman for Germany's Bundeskartellamt, the country's federal competition authority, told Reuters on Wednesday that it was maintaining close cooperation with the Commission inquiry.
"There will in no way be a conflict. We cooperate closely because it doesn't make sense to separate (our) inquiries," Elke Zeise said.
